subject: maths
title: Percentage change and compound interest

slides.heading: Percentage change — measuring how much things grow or shrink
slides.body: Percentage change expresses an increase or decrease as a proportion of the original value, making it possible to compare changes of different sizes fairly. The multiplier method is the most powerful tool: a 20% increase means multiply by 1.20; a 20% decrease means multiply by 0.80. Compound interest applies the multiplier repeatedly — each year's interest is calculated on the new total, not just the original, so the amount grows faster than simple interest.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: Percentage change and multipliers
slides.formula: % change = (change ÷ original) × 100 | Increase multiplier = 1 + (r/100) | Decrease multiplier = 1 − (r/100) | Compound: A = P × mⁿ
slides.formulaExplained: To find percentage change: subtract original from new to get the change, divide by the original, then multiply by 100. If positive it is an increase; if negative it is a decrease. For applying a % increase or decrease: multiply by 1 + r/100 (increase) or 1 − r/100 (decrease), where r is the percentage. For compound interest or depreciation: A = P × mⁿ, where P is the starting amount, m is the multiplier, and n is the number of periods. For reverse percentage (finding the original): divide the known value by the multiplier.
slides.whenToUse: Calculating % change between two values; applying a % increase or decrease to find a new value; finding the original value after a known % change (reverse percentage); and compound interest or depreciation over multiple periods.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: A coat was originally priced at £160. In a sale it costs £120. Calculate the percentage decrease.

steps.instruction: Divide the change by the original value.
Multiply by 100 to convert to a percentage.
Check using the multiplier: a 25% decrease means multiplying by 0.75. £160 × 0.75 = £120 ✓.

slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Dividing the change by the new value instead of the original — e.g. for a price rising from £40 to £50, calculating 10 ÷ 50 = 20% instead of 10 ÷ 40 = 25%.
mistakes.correction: Percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100. Always divide by the original (starting) value, not the new one.

mistakes.mistake: Reversing a percentage change by adding or subtracting the percentage directly — e.g. a TV costs £350 after a 30% reduction, so finding the original by adding 30% to £350 (£350 × 1.30 = £455) instead of dividing by 0.70.
mistakes.correction: After a 30% reduction, £350 = 70% of original. Reverse it by dividing by the multiplier: £350 ÷ 0.70 = £500. Adding the same percentage back undoes a percentage of the wrong base.

mistakes.mistake: Using simple interest instead of compound — e.g. for £2,000 at 4% for 3 years, calculating 4% × 3 = 12% total, giving £2,240 instead of applying the multiplier 1.04 three times to get £2,249.73.
mistakes.correction: Compound interest: multiply by the multiplier for each period separately — A = P × mⁿ. Simple interest adds the same fixed amount each time; compound always gives a higher result.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: % change = (change ÷ original) × 100. Change = new − original (positive = increase, negative = decrease). Always divide by the original.
keyFacts.examTip: The original is the starting value before the change — never the new value. This is the most common error in percentage change questions.

keyFacts.fact: Multiplier for r% increase: 1 + r/100. Multiplier for r% decrease: 1 − r/100. Reverse percentage: divide by the multiplier.
keyFacts.examTip: A 30% reduction gives multiplier 0.70. To reverse: ÷ 0.70 (not + 30%). Adding 30% back gives 30% of the reduced price, not the original.

keyFacts.fact: Compound growth/decay: A = P × mⁿ, where P = principal, m = multiplier, n = number of periods.
keyFacts.examTip: Write A = P × mⁿ and substitute before calculating. Use a calculator for mⁿ — do not round intermediate answers or compound errors build up.

keyFacts.fact: Simple interest gives the same fixed amount each period (I = PRT/100). Compound interest gives a larger total because each period's interest is added to the running total before the next calculation.
keyFacts.examTip: If a question says 'compound', use the multiplier method (× mⁿ). If it says 'simple', use I = PRT/100 and add the interest once at the end.
